title: Regret-Guided Search Control for Efficient Learning in AlphaZero
one_liner: AlphaZero learns faster by restarting from states where it made the worst mistakes, guided by a learned ranking of regret.
lead: Teaching a game-playing AI to learn efficiently like a human is hard. Humans improve rapidly by replaying moves where they went wrong; AlphaZero instead trains on random past states without preference. This paper adds a regret network that spots the states where AlphaZero's prediction was most wrong, then restarts self-play from those states, focusing learning effort where it matters most.

problem.h2: Learning from every state equally wastes training time
paras: When AlphaZero plays games against itself, most states it encounters are easy wins or obvious losses—the model's guess already matches reality. Only a handful of states truly matter: the ones where the model guessed wrong and learned something. But standard AlphaZero treats all states the same during retraining, restarting from the initial position and playing through the whole game again.

A human would do something smarter. After a game, a human player replays the exact moments where they miscalculated, not the whole game from the start. Each replay focuses on fixing the worst mistake. AlphaZero, without that focus, needs far more games to reach the same skill level.

callout.b: The core problem in one sentence:
callout.html: AlphaZero wastes learning by replaying states where it was already right, instead of restarting from states where it was most wrong.

steps.text: AlphaZero generates a full game and collects all states visited.
The regret network ranks states by how far the model's guess diverged from the real outcome.
States where regret was highest go into a ranked storage, sorted by regret value.

steps.b: Restart future games from these states
steps.text: Instead of always starting from the board's opening position, sometimes restart mid-game from a high-regret state.
The model learns faster because most new games now start where learning is needed most.

paras: The paper adds a restart buffer and a regret network. Normally AlphaZero replays any stored state uniformly at random. The regret network learns to rank states by regret, and only the highest-ranked states are selected for restart. This is a simple change to one choice: which past state to restart from.

hidden.h2: Regret: how wrong the model was
hidden.name: regret (prediction divergence)
paras: Regret is a single number per state that measures how badly the model's guess missed the truth. If AlphaZero predicted the agent would win with 90% confidence but actually lost, the regret is large (the gap between prediction and reality). If AlphaZero predicted a draw and got a draw, regret is near zero. The paper's key insight is that high-regret states hold the most learning signal: they show exactly where the model is broken.

The regret network is a small neural network that learns to estimate regret by seeing many states and their outcomes. It is trained with a ranking objective: assign high scores to the highest-regret states in any batch, using a temperature-scaled ranking. This ranking approach works better than directly predicting regret values, because most states have near-zero regret and direct prediction gets drowned out by noise.

heat.caption: Darker means higher regret. Bright squares are where the model was most wrong.

reads.html: Think of a chess player who missed a tactic and lost because of it. The regret of that position is how badly they missed it. High regret means a position where your mistake had big consequences.

Regret is the L2 norm between the value prediction from the old model and the actual outcome observed after the game ended. High-regret states are those where the agent's evaluation function was most inaccurate.

paras: The mechanism is straightforward. When a neural network learns, it learns fastest from examples where it is most confused. In AlphaZero, most past states are already well-predicted, so training on them wastes computation. By selecting only the states where the model was most wrong (high regret), every training step focuses on fixing actual errors instead of reinforcing correct guesses that do not need reinforcing.

When training restarts from a high-regret state mid-game, the model must immediately confront the exact situation it got wrong before. This collision between prediction and reality drives faster learning, because the model's training focus is forced onto the exact weak point instead of being diluted across easy states. The regret network learns which states are hardest by matching its scores to real prediction errors from finished games—it is trained on this data just like any other neural network. Concentrating training on hard states helps because those states contain the most information for updating the model—easy states waste training effort on patterns the model already knows. Over many games, the regret network's scoring becomes sharper as it sees more examples, so it picks out the truly hard states more accurately, leading to even more focused training.

stages.s: Rank by regret; store top 5 in buffer
Next training game restarts from buffer
Model retrains on high-error states fast

math.words: For a set of states in one game, compute a temperature-scaled exponential score for each regret value. This ranking assigns high scores to high-regret states. The ranking loss maximizes the expected regret under this scoring distribution, so the network learns to give high scores to the states with largest prediction errors.
math.equation: rho(s|S) = exp(gamma * regret_s) / sum_s' exp(gamma * regret_s'); J_rank = sum_s rho(s|S) * regret_s
symbols: probability assigned to state s from set S
how wrong the prediction was at state s
temperature scaling: higher gamma makes probabilities sharper
ranking objective: expected regret under the probability distribution
sum over all states in the batch

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a batch has 4 states with regrets: [0.1, 0.05, 0.6, 0.2]. Use gamma=1.
The ranking network learns that assigning high probability to high-regret states maximizes this objective.

math.note: The temperature-scaled exponential ranking makes low-regret states almost invisible, focusing all the learning effort on the rare states where the model was genuinely confused.

charts.title: Standard AlphaZero
charts.note: Learning is slow early because training includes many easy states where nothing new is learned.

charts.title: RGSC (Regret-Guided)
charts.note: Learning starts faster and continues steeper, because every training game restarts from states where the model is most confused.

items.b: Regret network overfits to early mistakes.
items.html: If the regret network is trained on only a few states, it may learn spurious patterns instead of genuine learning signals. This is why the paper uses a large regret buffer and ranking-based training.

If the model restarts from high-regret states too frequently (high restart rate), it may get stuck replaying old patterns and miss new winning strategies. The paper shows that very high restart rates cause instability in Hex.

items.b: Regret ranking assumes outcome ground truth.
items.html: High regret only makes sense when you know the true outcome after the game ends. In environments where the outcome is random or delayed, regret becomes noisy and the ranking loses power.

RGSC works best on deterministic board games where outcomes are clear, the model's error is measurable, and restarting from mid-game positions is valid. On Go, Othello, and Hex, it consistently improves speed because these are fully-observable games where regret is an unambiguous signal and mid-game restart is mechanically sound.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small RL agent that plays a simple game like Connect-4 or a tiny Checkers board (4x4). Implement three variants: (1) always restart from the opening, (2) restart from random past states (like Go-Exploit), (3) restart from states ranked by prediction error (RGSC). Train all three for the same number of games. Measure skill at regular intervals. Plot learning curves.
demo.metric_eq: Elo improvement = final_skill - initial_skill for each method after N training games
demo.closing: The RGSC plot should climb steeper and plateau higher than both baselines, proving that targeting high-error states accelerates learning.
